patches.new:
Conditions of worth force the child to distort their self-concept to match external expectations, creating incongruence between the real self and the ideal self.

Rogers described a second, more fundamental form of incongruence, and it is the one his theory actually rests on. Every person has an **organismic valuing process**: an innate, pre-verbal capacity to evaluate experiences by whether they genuinely further the person's own growth — what feels right, what feels wrong, what one actually wants. Conditions of worth teach the child to override that internal compass and judge experiences by whether they will earn approval instead. The result is a split between the **self-concept** (built from other people's conditions) and the **organismic valuing process** (what the person actually experiences and values). A person in this state can no longer tell what they want from what they are supposed to want; they defer, seek reassurance, and lose access to their own preferences. The real-self/ideal-self gap is the visible symptom; the self-concept drifting away from organismic experience is the underlying fault.
